Maintenance came up to cockpit and turned on screen and immediately got the strong electrical burning smell.
ASRSN:2278666.s: The crew returned to ZZZ shortly after departure when the Captain's PFD flickered and emitted an electrical burning smell at 7,000 feet. After landing safely, maintenance confirmed the odor originated from the recently replaced PFD, which they had installed following a prior dim screen report.

ASRSN:2278668.n: We left ZZZZ with the mid-lav inop. The proper calculations were made in regards to the number of paxs with 1-lav inop. My FO checked the lavs as best as a person can for the 757. We also received the notification that the lavs had been serviced in ZZZZ.2-hours into the flight, the fwd lav was already full. The decision to restrict first class paxs only to use this lav was made. All other would have to use the aft lavs. The FA in the back advised me that there was a steady line of paxs for the aft lavs for over an hour. A little while later, the aft FA advised me that both aft lavs were now full. We still had 4-hours left in the flight back to ZZZ.I had a satcom call with dispatch. He was not very helpful at all. We spoke with Maintenance Control and he confirmed the calculations were done correctly. No more help needed from Mx (Maintenance).We then asked dispatch for his opinion and he asked if we were thinking diversion. We said yes. His immediate suggestion was ZZZZ1. Yes it was closer than ZZZ1, however, he did not take into account customs, pax, and getting the services we needed.My FO and I wanted to divert to ZZZ1 because it is a large station for us, can comfortably accommodate our aircraft, and has US customs if needed. Dispatch agreed. Once again, dispatch was of little help.We asked dispatch for help to get us routing to ZZZ1. He said he couldn't and that we would have to do all of that coordination. Once again, dispatch was of little help. Me and my FO made contact with ATC and secured a new clearance to land in ZZZ1.Made it to ZZZ1 uneventfully and parked remotely. Mx immediately boarded the aircraft and confirmed that the mid-lav was labeled correctly as inoperable. Mx then informed us that the lavs had NOT been dumped in ZZZZ and that is why our lav tanks filled up so quickly. Ugh!!We spoke with the Chief Pilot and it was determined that we were not legal to proceed to DH (Dead Head) to ZZZ. Dispatch was very adamant that we were and to just stay on the plane and it will all work out. Nope!We cleared customs and then called the Dispatcher. They advised us that we were to DH to ZZZ that night. I spoke with her and advised her that I had spoken with the Chief Pilot, he had spoken with another Dispatcher and also the operations manager and we would need a hotel for the night. After a 15-minute wait, our pairing was updated and we were given a hotel for the night.We diverted because the lavs were full up to the flapper and were worried about a haz mat situation.Throughout this entire situation, we felt like there was little to no help from the dispatcher and that we were left on our own to accomplish a lot of things. He just kept saying it was our responsibility to do it. Dispatch was definitely not 1-stop shopping. It was also very challenging to communicate with dispatch because of a language barrier. His accent was so thick that we struggled to understand what was being said.
ASRSN:2278668.s: The crew of a Boeing 757 diverted to ZZZ1 during cruise because lavatory tanks filled prematurely due to failure to dump them at departure. Dispatch provided minimal assistance and communication was hindered by a language barrier, forcing the crew to coordinate the diversion and secure a hotel overnight.

ASRSN:2278746.n: During departure from ZZZ, the aircraft experienced an IRS (Inertial Reference System) Fault malfunction, which required crew action. FO as PF, CA as PM, aircraft established on ZZZZZ RNAV departure between FL180 and FL230. Initially, the autopilot engaged CWS (Control Wheel Steering) steering modes before disconnecting entirely as all navigation data was blanked from the FO screens. The crew recognized and communicated the faults to each other, transferred control of the aircraft to the CA, who still had information on his PFD (Primary Flight Display) and ND (Navigation Display). Autopilot was initially unable to reconnect. The crew coordinated with ATC to stop the climb and level at FL230 to work on the issue. With the CA as PF and FO as PM now, the crew completed the IRS FAULT QRH checklist, which restored data to the FO's screens. FPV (Flight Path Vector) and winds aloft data showed erroneous data on both sides (massive side slip, winds at FL230 in excess of 250 kts) so the crew determined the need to return to a field with vectors only. RNAV data could no longer be utilized for navigation. Checklist complete, the CA transferred controls to the FO and attempted to contact dispatch via crew phone. Unfortunately, the wifi system would not connect, so the CA advised dispatch via ACARS of the intention to return to ZZZ. FO coordinated with ATC for radar vectors to ZZZ and a descent, advising that the flight could not complete RNAV-specific navigation legs. The CA completed the Non-Routine Landing Considerations checklist, including notifying both the FAs and passengers of the flight status via intercom and PA, respectively. CA then completed the Overweight landing checklist in anticipation of landing at approximately 147.3k pounds.Checklists and communications complete the CA resumed PF duties because the nature of the system degradation gave priority to his screens, which would best enable a safe landing. The FO requested priority handling with ATC, and the flight landed XXC via the ILS. On approach, the crew completed the remaining checklist items, which included disabling the autopilot and autothrottles and reenabling the yaw damper. Autobrakes were inoperative due to the IRS Fault. Landing and rollout were uneventful, and the flight was escorted from the runway to the gate by vehicles as a precaution.Cause: The root cause of the event was an R IRS Fault that disabled flight data and navigation data on the FO's side of the aircraft. The crew mitigated via crew coordination, ATC assistance, TEM (Threat and Error Management), and the QRH. Recommend sustain current high standards of aircrew training, excellence in EFB (Electronic Flight Bag) and publication integration.
ASRSN:2278746.s: During departure from ZZZ, an R IRS fault blanked the FO's navigation displays, forcing a return to ZZZ with radar vectors and an overweight ILS landing. The crew mitigated the issue using QRH checklists and ATC coordination, resulting in an uneventful landing despite inoperative autobrakes.

ASRSN:2278784.n: We were approaching Runway XXR. On about a 5 mile final, tower had Aircraft Y line up and wait while the previous aircraft exited the runway. When we were at a 3 mile, Aircraft Z had cleared the runway and tower gave Aircraft Y takeoff clearance. Aircraft Y refused the takeoff clearance by stating 'unable' (they never stated the reason why before we switched back over to approach control). Tower initiated our go-around and we performed the go-around procedure per the go-around profile, followed by the appropriate checklists. We landed uneventfully on the second attempt.
ASRSN:2278784.s: While approaching Runway XXR, the crew executed a go-around after Aircraft Y refused takeoff clearance with "unable" at 3 miles final. The crew followed go-around procedures and checklists, landing uneventfully on the second attempt.

ASRSN:2278793.n: Departure off Runway XX. Assigned 230 heading. FO Flying. Initiated turn at approximately 800'. At around 1200' we received 'terrain' alert immediately followed by 'bank angle' and another 'terrain' as we were climbing through 1500.' FO had terrain up on his side I did not see any red and after 3-4 seconds there were no other alerts and climbout was normal. Terrain avoidance procedure was not initiated. ZZZ Tower cleared us for takeoff from Runway XX with a departure heading of 230°. VNAV was armed, and Terrain Display was selected on the FO side, as ZZZ is designated as a mountainous terrain airport. Takeoff proceeded normally, with gear retraction followed by the 'Heading' call at 400 feet. The turn to heading 230 was initiated shortly after, in accordance with departure takeoff bars on the PFD. A few seconds later, at approximately 1,000 -1,200 feet, a cyan 'APPR 2 NOT AVAIL' message appeared on the EICAS, accompanied by a yellow RA box. This was followed by 'Terrain' and 'Bank Angle' messages being annunciated aurally in the cockpit.We continued to follow the departure guidance, and all messages cleared within another split second. The rest of the flight proceeded normally, with no further alerts or indications.
ASRSN:2278793.s: The First Officer flew a departure from Runway XX, turning to heading 230° at 800 feet. At 1,200 feet, transient terrain and bank angle alerts triggered due to mountainous terrain, but the crew continued the climb without initiating avoidance procedures as the alerts cleared immediately.

ASRSN:2278800.n: Upon arrival into ZZZ, (after doors were disarmed and cross-checked), the gate agent that met the aircraft did not knock or even look in the door to see a 'thumbs up.' She walked up to the door and opened it. When she got it all the way open, I said 'you need to knock and look for a thumbs up.' She chuckled and said 'oh ok!
ASRSN:2278800.s: A cabin crew member reported that a gate agent opened the aircraft door at ZZZ without knocking or checking for a thumbs-up signal after doors were disarmed. The crew member corrected the agent, who acknowledged the error.

ASRSN:2278913.n: I was working on a routine overnight inspection for Aircraft X at DCA while it was on a gate. Me and two other co-workers saw that we had a main landing gear tire to change and a Inbound issue that we needed to change both nose landing gear tires. After performing an oil servicing task on engine Person A came up to me and discussed that he would do the walk around and Person B would change the main tire, and asked if I could go up and start the paperwork. I went up stairs through the jet bridge to get to the aircraft. Person B who was down by the MLG called up to me while I was halfway up the stairs saying that he was ready for me to release the brakes. I went up into the aircraft, applied power and waited for the flight control power up test to finish. When the (P-BIT) Power-on Built-in Test finished I proceeded to release the parking brake. I then felt the plane move more than it should have, which later was found to be that the aircraft had moved back less than a foot and stopped. I went down the jet bridge over to where my coworkers Person B and Person A were to find that Person A had removed all of the chocks from the nose landing gear from and main landing gear before telling me to release the brake and had placed a chock down behind the main landing gear that he had been getting ready to work on after he noticed it move more than it should have. I went back upstairs inspected the area around the forward passenger door, I then went back downstairs to talk with my co-workers about what had happened. After talking I found out that Person B had removed the chocks on the R/H MLG which he was about to start changing a tire on and the nose landing gear from which we had an inbound issue to take care of. Person B had not checked the L/H MLG to see if there were chocks on those tires before telling me to release the parking brake. I was unaware that the chocks had been removed when I released the parking brake after having been told to release the parking brake when I went upstairs. When we were downstairs discussing the event I notified my shift supervisor Person C about what had occurred. He called Operations to get them to move the jet bridge back into position. Person C also inspected the plane. Our supervision told us when we got back to the office to file a report for what had happened. We saw no damage to the aircraft or to equipment. All personal were not injured. On the aircraft listed above I was going to change a MLG tire which requires the brakes to be released. I pulled the chocks from under the RH MLG tire so the aircraft would not catch them when we lower the aircraft after removal and replacement of the tires. I also to try to save time was preparing the NLG tires to be replaced as well and removed the NLG chocks. Just as I was about to start jacking the aircraft from the MLG I told 1 of my co-workers to release the break. I finished setting up for the MLG tire to begin jacking and the brakes were released. The plane began to roll back a bit from where it was parked and I kept calm and placed one of the MLG chocks right behind the tire I was about to begin working on and the plane came to a stop. After looking over how far the aircraft had moved from its original parking spot which is about a little under a foot I told my co-workers that we should probably contact our supervisor to let him know what had happened. After looking everything over we noticed nothing had been damaged on the aircraft, tools, or equipment. It could have been a lot worse. Thankfully it wasn't and I now have learned to not try to speed things up from the maintenance manual directions.
ASRSN:2278913.s: During an overnight inspection at DCA, maintenance personnel removed landing gear chocks and released the parking brake to change tires, causing the aircraft to roll back less than a foot. The incident resulted in no damage or injuries, attributed to rushing the procedure and failing to verify chock status before brake release.

ASRSN:2278924.n: Pre-flight inspection and briefing completed in accordance with 14 CFR 91.103. Six quarts of oil observed in both engines. Fuel quantity verified at fifty gallons per wing (one hundred total). No discrepancies noted during pre-flight, engine start, taxi, or run-up.Departed ZZZ runway XX from intersection 1 on a VFR south departure. Takeoff was normal with all indications in the green. Climbed to the south practice area and maneuvered at approximately 4,500 feet MSL. During throttle adjustments, the right engine manifold pressure gauge exhibited intermittent sticking on three occasions, but remained responsive. Condition assessed as a possible instrumentation anomaly.During a steep turn maneuver, the right engine (engine two) developed significant roughness. Engine failure procedures initiated. Troubleshooting checklist accomplished with no corrective effect. Indications observed: right oil pressure decreasing toward the yellow/red range, cylinder head temperature above normal, fuel pressure normal, white smoke visible from right engine.Decision made to secure engine two. Propeller feathered, mixture cutoff, and engine secure checklist completed. Requested priority handling with Approach and reported single-engine operations inbound to ZZZ.Intercepted the localizer for runway XY and conducted a stabilized single-engine approach, maintaining airspeed. Normal landing accomplished on runway XY. Aircraft exited at taxiway 2 and shut down. Aircraft was hand-towed to ramp and secured.No injuries, no collateral damage, no additional assistance required., "Prior to push back, the Captain and I 'chair flew' the new Date SOPs to include actions/call outs for Engine Loss at V1 and CAT 1 ILS and Engine Out Approach/Landing and Go Arounds. This timely review significantly reduced our workload in flight and reduced the number of errors committed during the ensuing situation given the otherwise lack of training on the new SOPs.Climbing through 17,000 ft. we heard a loud bang and felt a jolt to the aircraft followed by an ENG 2 STALL ECAM. The stall cleared itself in less than 5 seconds. Captain/Pilot Monitoring referenced the QRH procedure. The Flight Attendants and a Pilot riding in the cabin informed us that a Visual Flame was observed in the #2 Engine associated with the Compressor Stall, but no external damage was observable. Engine was returned to normal operation following completion of the QRH procedure. At 35,000 ft., approaching Top of Descent, the #2 engine experienced a second series of Stalls. The Stalls included an ECAM ENG 2 STALL Message, Erratic EPR Indications, Audible Banging and Visual Flames as reported visually, again from the cabin. The First Officer/Pilot Flying immediately retarded the Thrust Lever and the Stall cleared. Captain/Pilot Monitoring called ATC for a decent and executed QRH procedure. We elected to operate the #2 Engine at idle power for the duration of the flight. We requested priority handling with Center and requested a descent and expedited approach to ZZZ. 'Non-routine landing considerations' were reviewed and a precautionary landing was conducted to XXC. Fire/safety personnel inspected the aircraft after landing and indicated no visible damage. Priority handling was terminated and we taxied to the gate.Landing with one engine at IDLE thrust after running the QRH procedure is somewhat confusing. While not technically a single engine approach, we treated it as such (since it could turn into one at any second). It would be helpful if the Engine Stall checklist directed a reference to 'Approach Considerations' on the QRH. This section is difficult to find in the heat of battle."
ASRSN:2278924.s: Two separate incidents involved pilots experiencing right engine issues: one pilot secured an engine due to roughness and smoke during a VFR practice flight, while another crew managed repeated compressor stalls with visual flames on a jet, operating the engine at idle for a precautionary landing.

ASRSN:2278930.n: Day 0, I went out on a flight with a friend to practice my instructing skills as I am currently a CFI student. We went southeast of the airfield, and I practiced teaching various maneuvers. Then we came back to ZZZ, our origin airfield, for some pattern work. After my first touch-and-go on Runway XX, at 500 ft AGL on the upwind, I raised my flaps to cruise configuration, and the airframe began to shake violently. I visually inspected both flaps, and they appeared to be normal. In response, I returned my flaps to the T/O configuration they were previously in, something that isn't typical procedure in the DA20-C1. I made the decision that I had to make my next landing full stop, as this was an unfamiliar situation and not something I had ever been trained on. While in the downwind, I tried troubleshooting by experimenting with various flap configurations, but the cruise flaps setting was still consistently producing violent shaking. This first hole in the Swiss Cheese Model, admittedly, led to considerable task saturation. I became fixated on gaining altitude and airspeed while still having flaps in due to the fear of causing the shaking to occur again when I raised my flaps, meanwhile ensuring that the engine was functioning normally. In this highly task-saturated downwind leg, I failed to take note of an arriving Citation CJ3+. They entered an extended left base for XX, and as they began to establish on short final, I began to enter my left base for XX. Upon turning base, I made visual contact with the Citation and pitched up to avoid getting in its flight path. If I had continued on my descent path without seeing them, it wouldn't have resulted in a mid-air collision, however, it would've been too close for comfort. The approximate closest distance between us was about 1500 feet horizontal, 500 feet vertical. This is a great lesson on how high-stress situations, such as abnormal shaking of the airframe due to a flap issue, can result in the inability to make accurate perceptions. As an instrument-rated commercial pilot, this mistake is an embarrassing but incredibly valuable lesson. The impact on perceptions that the stress of an abnormal situation in flight can have on the pilot is drastic. This was a wake-up call that taught me the importance of maintaining traffic separation at the top of my priorities- aviate (avoid traffic), navigate, communicate. Ultimately, this mistake served as an incredibly valuable lesson in showing me how I personally respond to alarming situations in the air. I'm grateful that everyone is safe and that I can move on from this situation as a better pilot. I look forward to ensuring my future students don't make the same mistake.
ASRSN:2278930.s: A CFI student in a DA20-C1 experienced violent shaking at 500 ft AGL after raising flaps, causing task saturation during pattern work at ZZZ. This distraction led to a loss of situational awareness regarding an arriving Citation CJ3+, resulting in a close call with 1,500 feet horizontal and 500 feet vertical separation.

ASRSN:2278931.n: An aborted takeoff was performed as we took the runway. I was the pilot flying at the time. As we lined up on runway XX, and were cleared for takeoff, I continued my normal procedures as usual. When the captain handed me the flight controls, I acknowledged the flight controls and began to increase thrust on both engines to take off power. Within moments, I noticed the left engine N1 had increased to around 60%, where the right engine N1 was displaying 30%. The right engine was not spooling up, and since we were at a slow speed, I acknowledged it and told the captain. We called for an aborted takeoff on the runway due to engine abnormality, and safely exited the runway at the next intersection. After completing the aborted takeoff checklist, we requested to run some tests in the runup area to see if the problem persisted. Once at the runup area, we increased both thrust levers and the right engine was still not spooling up to takeoff thrust. We taxi back to the FBO, grounded the airplane and wrote it up. Maintenance is looking at the plane.
ASRSN:2278931.s: The pilot flying aborted takeoff on runway XX after the right engine failed to spool up while the left reached 60% N1. The aircraft was grounded at the FBO after confirming the right engine still would not reach takeoff thrust during runup tests.

ASRSN:2278936.n: I was in cruise phase level at 4,000' direct CHA out of ZZZ. Heading 080. On IFR flight plan (round robin: ZZZ to CHA back to ZZZ).I was doing an engine break-in (only had about 9 hours SMOH) so my head was down in the cockpit more than normal. I was approximately within 5nm of Stevenson (7A6) when I looked up and directly ahead was what looked like twin black diamonds, joined together, heading directly towards me. Before I had time to react, it was past me - went directly overhead at about 200' above.I saw it only for about 2-3 seconds, did not even have time to disconnect the autopilot or engage in evasive maneuvers. The object appeared to be about 4-6 feet long and looked like a drone or possibly a box kite. Impossible to ascertain the object's speed or heading.There was nothing on my ADS-B In.
ASRSN:2278936.s: A pilot conducting an engine break-in at 4,000 feet reported a near-miss with an unidentified object resembling a drone or box kite while approaching Stevenson. The object passed overhead at approximately 200 feet above the aircraft, leaving no time for evasive action and appearing on no ADS-B In display.

ASRSN:2278945.n: On Day 0, I was conducting my second solo flight at ZZZ to practice local practice area. Before departure, I did a complete pre-flight inspection along with my instructor checking the control surfaces, fuel quantity, oil levels, tires, and general condition of the aircraft. Everything was normal and in working order. Then I was cleared to taxi to Runway XX via taxiway 1. I completed the engine run-up and all pre-takeoff checks in the run up area. Oil pressure and temperature were in the green, magnetos checked and working properly, and the mixture was set to full rich.I taxied on to Runway XX, aligned on the centerline, and began my takeoff roll. The aircraft accelerated normally, and I rotated at 55 knots. Initially, the climb was normal and the aircraft was responding well. However, when the aircraft reached about 200 feet above ground level, there was a sudden loss of power. The aircraft wasn't climbing and I could not gain altitude. I quickly verified that the throttle was full forward, the mixture was full rich, and both magnetos were on, but nothing improved the situation.Realizing I did not have enough altitude to continue climbing safely and no safe landing spot ahead of me I made the decision to turn back to the runway. I executed a 180-degree turn to line up with Runway XY I also let the ATC know about the situation trying to manage airspeed and altitude carefully while keeping the aircraft under control.I touched down at the intersection of Runway XY and Taxiway 2. The landing caused the aircraft to bounce slightly, and it continued rolling until coming to a stop near the end of Runway XZ. During the landing, the left main tire went flat due to the bounce. Throughout the incident, I focused on maintaining control and avoiding obstacles, and I was able to stop the aircraft safely. The aircraft was towed to the ramp by the maintenance. There was no damage to the airframe, power plant and the occupant.
ASRSN:2278945.s: A student pilot experienced sudden power loss at 200 feet AGL during a solo training takeoff at ZZZ. The pilot executed a 180-degree turn and landed on Runway XY, resulting in a flat left main tire but no damage to the airframe, power plant, or occupant.

ASRSN:2278947.n: This was the first flight after annual. During my descent and vectors into ZZZ I began feeling light headed around 7000 feet while getting vectored around Class B of ZZZ1 to the east. This made me look over to the other side of the instrument panel to my CO (Carbon Monoxide) card which had turned black. The heater was not on, at this point I opened the pilot window for airflow and advised ATC that I believed to be experiencing a Carbon Monoxide event and requested to land at ZZZ2 ASAP. The approach and landing was uneventful.
ASRSN:2278947.s: The pilot experienced lightheadedness at 7,000 feet during descent into ZZZ1 after an annual inspection, confirmed by a blackened CO card. The pilot opened the window, notified ATC of a suspected Carbon Monoxide event, and landed safely at ZZZ2.

ASRSN:2278957.n: We departed uneventfully from ZZZ. Upon climbing through around 5,000 ft on the ZZZZ X SID, both pilots noticed visible white smoke in the cockpit accompanied by the smell of smoke. The 3 passengers on board also verbally alerted us (flight crew) of visible smoke. We then donned our oxygen masks and requested priority handling. ATC asked where we would like to go and we requested nearby ZZZ1. We were then given vectors for the ILS Runway XX to ZZZ1. We informed the 3 passengers on board of our intentions verbally over the cockpit speaker system. The airport was acquired visually, and upon notification of ATC we were cleared the visual approach Runway XX. The landing was uneventful, and we then taxied off the runway and stopped on Taxiway 1. ATC asked where we would like to go and we requested to shut down and deplane in place. With the parking brake set and engines shut down, and all passengers and crew promptly evacuated the airplane.
ASRSN:2278957.s: Flight crew and three passengers experienced visible smoke and odor at 5,000 ft during climb on the ZZZZ X SID. The crew donned oxygen masks, diverted to ZZZ1 for a visual approach to Runway XX, and evacuated the aircraft after shutting down on Taxiway 1.

ASRSN:2278958.n: When thermalling 3 miles south of ZZZ airport at 4000 feet I heard a pop and felt my roll control become very stiff. After recovering the aircraft from a near uncontrolled roll, I immediately diverted to ZZZ Airport, three miles away. Report filed.
ASRSN:2278958.s: A pilot thermalling 3 miles south of ZZZ airport at 4000 feet heard a pop and experienced stiff roll control. After recovering from a near uncontrolled roll, the pilot diverted to ZZZ Airport.

ASRSN:2278960.n: At XA:07, my student and I were conducting pattern work at ZZZ, making continuous radio calls on each leg. Aircraft Z departed Runway XX while we were established on the left downwind. We maintained visual contact. As we turned base to final, Aircraft Y was also on downwind, and our traffic alert activated as he was approximately 200 feet below and about half a mile horizontally from us. Both my student and I had the aircraft in sight. Shortly after, Aircraft Y turned base on a collision course with our aircraft. I immediately took control, initiated a climb and right turn into a go-around, side-stepping to the right for separation. He later apologized on XXX.X.
ASRSN:2278960.s: The pilot and student conducting pattern work at ZZZ executed a go-around and right turn when Aircraft Y turned base on a collision course while 200 feet below. The pilot initiated the maneuver after the traffic alert activated, resulting in separation and a subsequent apology from Aircraft Y on the radio.

ASRSN:2278985.n: Departing from ZZZ - ZZZ1 only crew (2) reposition flight. ETD XA:00, conditions were poor (night, weather). During initial climb, the FO reported smoke in the cockpit. We donned oxygen mask and began troubleshooting according to the QRH, ATC was advised. The smoke was identified as oil smoke. Shortly after, we observed the left engine oil pressure dropping abnormally. As a precautionary measure, and in accordance with the engine oil pressure low checklist, we shut down the left engine. ATC was notified and we requested vectors to the nearest suitable airport with ILS, good weather and long runway. We received vectors and conditions and proceeded to land safety at ZZZ2. The approach and landing were uneventful, and we taxied clear without further issues. Post-flight maintenance inspection and follow-up are pending. No injuries to the crew.
ASRSN:2278985.s: During the initial climb of a two-crew reposition flight in poor night weather, the First Officer reported oil smoke and left engine oil pressure loss. The crew shut down the left engine, diverted to ZZZ2, and landed safely with no injuries.

ASRSN:2279001.n: While landing from an ifr flight in VMC conditions to runway 34 at CLW, while short final to runway 34)estimated distance above ground to be 139 feet) Aircraft Y Announced he would be departing 34. I immediately guarded the controls and was under the impression he was simply announcing his attentions as i was already almost over the numbers landing 34. to the shock of myself and all others that witnessed, Aircraft Y decided to cut right out in front of me and depart runway 34. I immediately initiated a go around and was believed to have come about 130 feet over the top of the offending airplane. While in the climb out to rejoin the pattern, i asked multiple times why this had happened and got no response. I entered the downwind and landed runway 34 without further incident. When i walked into the FBO, i had multiple witnesses approach me and say they saw the whole thing and were scared on how close of a call it was. I submit this report in confidence and hope this pilot knows what he did and exactly how close this was to being a serious casuality. I do not believe weather to be a factor as the ceilings were 1900 above the pattern altitude.
ASRSN:2279001.s: The pilot landing on runway 34 at CLW initiated a go-around after Aircraft Y unexpectedly departed the runway directly in front of them at approximately 139 feet AGL. The reporter estimates passing about 130 feet above the departing aircraft and attributes the near-miss to the other pilot's unannounced maneuver rather than weather conditions.

ASRSN:2279048.n: After takeoff from ZZZ talking with ZZZ center on an IFR flight, I experienced a total electrical and avionics failure including the PFD's (Primary Flight Display) on both the PIC's side and SIC's (Second in Command) side. Flying with only a standby instrument and wet compass. Unable to communicate with center, I descended through an opening in the clouds down to VMC conditions. After running several checklists and trying to reset everything, I was eventually able to get a radio operating and communicated with ZZZ approach. They gave me priority handling since I was dealing with many failures and was able to safely land in ZZZ1 without any incidents. Since I was flying most of the way on a standby instrument and the wet compass, my altitudes and headings varied.
ASRSN:2279048.s: The pilot experienced a total electrical and avionics failure, including both PFDs, shortly after takeoff on an IFR flight. Unable to communicate initially, the crew descended to VMC using standby instruments, eventually contacted ZZZ approach for priority handling, and landed safely at ZZZ1 with varied altitudes and headings.

ASRSN:2279076.n: While operating under Part 107, I received LAANC authorization for a grid near El Paso International Airport. After flight completion, I reviewed my telemetry and realized that due to app lag/incorrect pin placement, I had actually flown in adjacent Class C airspace that was not covered by my authorization. The operation was brief, under 400ft altitude, and no conflicts with manned aircraft were observed. The error was unintentional and discovered only after the flight. In the future, I will cross-check LAANC authorizations with the FAA's B4UFLY app and verify grid location before launch to prevent recurrence., "My Student and I were doing pattern work on Runway 26 at Redlands. We were on right crosswind climbing when I noticed ADS-B traffic on my I-Pad very close and indicating 100 feet above same direction, there was no radio communication from them. I could not see them visually so we descended, they continued to indicate very close. I lifted my right wing and saw them a few hundred feet to my right. At first I thought they were entering the pattern at Redlands. They continued on what looked like a wide right crosswind for 26 Redlands. They turned right, I followed. Then they turned right again and made a descending 270 in front of me and headed for Runway 24 SBD. We are having increasing numbers of SBD aircraft in the Redlands pattern. This was an extremely dangerous situation which might have been avoided If the Tower at SBD had radar to better monitor traffic."
ASRSN:2279076.s: A Part 107 drone pilot unintentionally entered adjacent Class C airspace near El Paso due to app lag and incorrect pin placement, while a flight instructor and student at Redlands experienced a dangerous conflict with an SBD aircraft on a wide right crosswind due to lack of radar monitoring at SBD.

ASRSN:2279081.n: Shortly after assuming the position, Aircraft X, who was IFR conducting a practice approach to Runway 21 at CHO departed on a Tower assigned heading of 090. The scratchpad showed Z2E, indicating that the aircraft was going to conduct the RNAV Z 21 then depart to the east. The controller that I relieved later confirmed that the aircraft was issued the climb out instructions, 'fly Tower assigned heading, maintain 4,000' as required by the CHO Tower LOA (Letter of Agreement). The LOA also states that Tower must issue all IFR departures runway heading.The MVA east of CHO is 030. The Tower's issuance of the 090 heading did not comply with the MVA and put me in a position where an MVA violation had already occurred. No coordination was attempted by the Tower or I would have denied the heading as I do every time they ask, which they do frequently with IFR departures when they have a faster departure they need to get out behind them.When Aircraft X departed I noticed a 1200 code east of the field westbound indicating 030 +/- 100ft or so I issued traffic. It became apparent that Aircraft X was not going to be able the reach the MVA to be turned away from the traffic in time and they were on converging courses. I issued a traffic alert and advised Aircraft X to turn left immediately. I informed them that the MVA in that area was 030 but the traffic was at 030 so if they were able to stay at 025 it would keep them below the traffic, knowing the MVA would be 1;000ft above any actual obstructions. Because of the Tower's actions, the only option I had to avoid a collision was to turn the aircraft below the MVA and/or restrict them to an altitude below the MVA.This is not the first time this has occurred with CHO Tower, yet they still request turns for IFR departures or turn them with no coordination at all. I think they are under the impression that the scratchpad entry ending with an 'E' or 'W' authorizes them to turn an IFR below the MVA. Recommendation1. The LOA with CHO Tower needs to be updated to clearly state that practice approaches will be assigned runway heading. This should be done by the TRACON as part of the climb out instructions.2. The LOA with CHO Tower needs to be undated so that the 'W' and 'E' scratchpad entries are not entered for IFR practice approaches, only VFR.3.Both the Tower and the TRACON need to receive training that makes it clear that neither facility can turn an aircraft below the MVA. There must be PCT controllers still approving these turns or they would not be asking and I have seen the Tower launch fast departures behind slow moving departures not understanding that we cant turn them until they reach the MVA.4. A SID needs to be developed that (even if it includes climb rate requirements due to mountainous terrain) allows the Tower to assign divergent headings to subsequent departures. The LOA will need to be updated to either require verbal coordination for these headings or allow the use of the rundown list for this coordination., "Enroute ZZZ to ZZZ1, we were notified by Dispatch that ZZZ Operations loaded four aircraft slides into Bin XX without his knowledge or notifying us via the Dangerous Goods form. We clarified that the weight was correctly inputted into the performance data. We made the appropriate release correction and continued to ZZZ1."
ASRSN:2279081.s: An air traffic controller reported that CHO Tower issued an IFR departure heading of 090 for Aircraft X, violating the 030 MVA and creating a conflict with westbound traffic. The controller avoided a collision by instructing the aircraft to turn left and descend below the MVA, attributing the incident to a lack of coordination and non-compliance with the Letter of Agreement.

ASRSN:2279137.n: Climbing out of DEN we were assigned direct STAKR. Passing 12;000ft I saw a square, orange and white drone approximately 2ft by 2ft pass from 12 o'clock to 11 o'clock and within 200ft. No maneuvering occurred.
ASRSN:2279137.s: During climb out of DEN on a direct to STAKR, the crew observed a 2ft by 2ft orange and white drone pass within 200ft at 12,000ft. No evasive maneuvers were required.

ASRSN:2279232.n: Two weeks ago I departed Lima @ XA:30am on flight ABCD. We were informed after take-off by Lima Radar that a drone had been spotted around the Gelim intersection at around 8000ft moving west to east. We were in the area and ultimately didn't ever see the drone. Yesterday, I departed Lima, Peru from RW16L on the same flight and on the departure before Gelim at 5000ft we struck an indeterminate object coming from the south just aft of the radome on the underside of the aircraft. We didn't experience any adverse reaction to the encounter and after consultation with dispatch we continued the flight without incident. I wrote up the incident in the Logbook as a suspected bird strike. Due to the high closure rate of the object, I wasn't able to get a clean look, but suspect it was probably a drone due to the size and the altitude in which we struck the object. I believe this is a burgeoning threat in the Lima area and I am concerned that if this trend continues this could be a serious threat to aviation safety.The only way to mitigate the risks in this particular situation is to remove the threat of drones in the area.
ASRSN:2279232.s: The pilot reported striking an indeterminate object at 5,000ft near Gelim during departure from Lima, suspecting it was a drone based on size and altitude. Although no adverse reaction occurred and the flight continued, the pilot identified this as a growing safety threat requiring drone removal in the area.

ASRSN:2279270.n: Engine oil had been checked at end of each fly day prior to this flight. Dipstick showed sufficient oil on each check. Aircraft flew from ZZZ1 to ZZZ with no abnormal indications. Aircraft departed at XA:42 from ZZZ. During climb out from ZZZ to FL330 LH engine showed slightly less pressure than RH Engine, but still within limits. Oil pressure slowly bled off inflight until it reached 40 psi. At approximately XC:10 the LH OIL PRESS LOW caution light illuminated with Master Warning light. Per emergency checklist, crew initiated engine shutdown, informed ZZZ Center, and began drift down descent to FL250. After discussing options, PIC (Pilot in Command) opted to continue to ZZZ1. When fuel imbalance reached approximately 300 lbs, crew initiated fuel transfer from LH tank to RH engine. While monitoring fuel level, crew observed RH fuel quantity continued to drop, while LH fuel quantity remained the same. PIC elected to divert to ZZZ2, which had just been overflown. Executed a single-engine approach and landing to Runway XXR at ZZZ2. After shutdown crew noted there was still oil on dipstick, although engine had only been windmilling. There was an excessive amount of oil in rear of engine (aft of turbine section) in engine exhaust area, not in bypass area.
ASRSN:2279270.s: The crew of a twin-engine aircraft experienced a left engine oil pressure drop and low pressure warning during climb, prompting an emergency shutdown and diversion to ZZZ2. Despite sufficient oil on the dipstick, excessive oil was found in the engine exhaust area after a single-engine landing.

ASRSN:2279272.n: Cleared for a visual approach to RW 35 in SLC from waypoint HLMET. I chose and briefed the RNAV (GPS) Rwy 35 as a backup, and to practice my RNAV approach procedures as the LDA 35 was not in the navigation database. I was fully configured for landing at the final approach fix (FAF) KERNN at 6100 ft MSL. Waypoint WEEEL was not in the database, but I did brief that it was 1.9 miles from the end of the runway, and that it was required to track the approach course to wheel before turning to align with the landing runway, which is a 5.05 degree offset. Maybe because WEEEL was not in the database, I began a 1000-1200 fpm descent to the LNAV Cat C minimums at the FAF, thus going below the at or above 4900 altitude at WEEEL. We received an altitude alert from the Tower. I disconnected the autopilot and began a climb to visually transition to the PAPI lights, which were in view throughout the final approach. I told myself in my head, and even verbalized to an inquiring FO, that we were low on the PAPI lights because we were still short of the Visual Descent Point (VDP), which is located .9 miles from the end of the runway. I subsequently re-established a proper approach path and runway alignment and an uneventful landing. Crew Errors: 1). At the FAF, 4900 feet should have been selected until passing WEEEL where a descent to minimums could be initiated. Both pilots failed to notice this oversight.2). Since we were at or below 500 feet AGL and not on a normal approach path for landing, a go around should have been called for by either pilot, and initiated by the CA who was the pilot flying. From the FAF, I could have very easily tracked the course to WEEEL and just followed the PAPI lights as they were clearly in sight, but I wanted to practice a simulated LNAV approach. Missing the 4900 foot restriction at WEEEL lead to the approach path deviations. Also, since we were cleared for a visual approach, we could have used the LDA 35 as a backup to the visual approach with course and glide path guidance (green needles). Lessons learned: Don't hesitate to go around if the approach doesn't look right or if stabilized approach criteria are not met. Also, make sure that all of the PM calls are made which require a PF response and can be used to trap errors. Cause: Failure to maintain a minimum altitude (4900 at WEEEL) inside the final approach fix. Failure as a crew to verify that the requested VNAV altitude was selected.Suggestions: Especially in VFR conditions and cleared for a visual approach, use ALL available resources to maintain proper course and path. Strict adherence to company Standard Operating Procedures.
ASRSN:2279272.s: The pilot flying and first officer descended below the 4900 ft minimum at WEEEL while practicing a simulated RNAV approach during a visual approach to SLC RW 35. This crew error caused an altitude alert, requiring a climb to re-establish the path before an uneventful landing.

ASRSN:2279278.n: In cruise at FL220 aural warning pressurization 10000 red flashed with MASTER cabin alert flash. We both checked and confirmed EICAS message and donned oxygen masks and complied with QRC checklist. CA initiated emergency descent to 10000 and I requested priority handling with ATC. After reaching 10000, CA gave me control of the aircraft and radios and CA set up our diversion to ZZZ and communicated with company. We made our way to ZZZ with no further issues and landed ILS RXX. Taxied off without issue, gate XX. In cruise flight. 22,000 feet - master warning cabin alert. Donned crew oxygen masks, and complied with QRC emergency descent checklist. At this time we were within 20 miles of ZZZ. Transfer flight controls and radios to FO. Requested priority with ATC, messaged dispatch about the depressurization and diversion. Notified the flight attendant and passengers of the situation. Normal approach and landing into ZZZ. Trucks standing by but no assistance needed. Got to the gate and called dispatch, Maintenance and chief pilot. Passengers deplaned to await new aircraft inbound from ZZZ1. All 3 crew members unfit to continue.
ASRSN:2279278.s: The flight crew experienced a cabin depressurization at FL220, triggering a master warning and requiring an emergency descent to 10,000 feet. They diverted to ZZZ, landed safely, and all three crew members were declared unfit to continue.

ASRSN:2279321.n: I informed the purser and copilot to have Maintenance come see 1R slide. Slide was in brackets and secured but the slide had excess dragging on the floor.
ASRSN:2279321.s: The crew reported that the 1R slide, though secured in brackets, was dragging on the floor. Maintenance was requested to inspect the slide.

ASRSN:2279446.n: Coming in to land I was in control of the aircraft, but upon touchdown the plane pulled to the left immediately and I lost directional controls. I was completely off the rudders and brakes and the plane was still pulling to the left. I released controls of the aircraft to my instructor and she attempted to gain control again by using right rudder, but the plane continued pulling to the left off of the runway on to the grass and then back onto a closed taxiway. My instructor then pulled the mixture to come to a complete stop as we were not slowing down. We contacted tower straight away and they gave us priority handling. The airport ground crew was then sent to tow us to the FBO. The aircraft was able to be towed, so the left tire and brake were not locked. The FBO's mechanic inspected the tire and plate and there was no visible damage. The aircraft has 24.0 hours OFF/ON Hobbs time. His initial assessment was that because the aircraft was so new the brake pads and piston were tight and improperly lubricated that it caused a momentary lock up. Coming in to land my student was on the controls of the aircraft. Upon touchdown the plane immediately pulled to the left and directional controls was lost. I was completely off the rudders and brakes and the plane was still pulling to the left. I immediately took controls of the aircraft and tried to gain longitudinal alignment and control by using right rudder, but the plane continued pulling to the left off of the runway up on to the grass and then back onto a closed taxiway. Having no brake authority I then had to pull the mixture in order to come to a stop. We contacted tower straight away and they requested priority handling on our behalf. The airport ground crew was then sent to tow us to the FBO. The aircraft was able to be towed, so the left tire and brake were not locked. The FBO's mechanic inspected the aircraft and there was no visible damage to the tires. The aircraft has 24.0 OFF/ON Hobbs time. His initial assessment and determination was that because the aircraft was so new the brake pads and piston were tight and improperly lubricated which caused the momentary lock up.
ASRSN:2279446.s: A student pilot and instructor landed a new aircraft with 24.0 Hobbs hours when the left brake locked due to tight, improperly lubricated pads, causing a runway excursion onto grass and a closed taxiway. The instructor stopped the aircraft using the mixture control, and ground crew towed it to the FBO with no visible damage found.

ASRSN:2279447.n: I was performing practice approaches for currency at the ZZZ in a Cirrus SR20. Those on board included myself, a safety pilot and one passenger in the rear seat. During the execution of the published missed approach procedure for the ILS Runway XX I elected to divert to ZZZ1 for additional practice approaches due to increased traffic at ZZZ.At the time of breaking off from the published missed approach, the aircraft was approximately two nautical miles southwest of the ZZZ airfield at an altitude of 2500 ft MSL. A climb was initiated during the transition to a course for ZZZ1. Upon throttle up for climb, the engine sputtered and ceased producing significant thrust. At the time of engine failure, the aircraft was approximately 3.5 nautical miles southwest of the approach end of Runway XX at ZZZ.An immediate turn back toward Runway XX at ZZZ was initiated and priority handling was requested. Once on course for Runway XX, it was observed that all four PAPI lights were white indicating a high approach path. The aircraft was pitched for best glide speed and successfully landed on Runway XX.The landing was uneventful, with no injuries to pilot or passengers, and no damage to the aircraft. Sufficient momentum remained to roll the aircraft off of the runway and onto the parking apron. Training received during PPL course was instrumental in effectively managing this scenario. Without training, evaluation of the available options, and taking decisive action to ensure safety of passengers would present a potentially insurmountable challenge.
ASRSN:2279447.s: The pilot of a Cirrus SR20 experienced an engine failure during a climb after diverting from a missed approach at ZZZ. The crew executed a successful emergency landing on Runway XX with no injuries or damage, attributing the safe outcome to prior training.

ASRSN:2279453.n: Wind gust on landing ground looped after touchdown exited runway on to grass knocked runway light over. shut down immediately thinking we had blown tire and or aircraft damage. Gave thumbs up to police helicopter who was talking to tower. After observing no immediate emergency turned on radio notified tower of situation ask to exit aircraft to see if blown tire then got back on radio notified all ok but would wait for FBO truck to tow us in. After FBO truck declined to tow us we got on phone with tower ask for permission to go back to aircraft be and pull by hand to taxiway at that point we would start up and then call him for permission to taxi back to hanger if all systems ok. They were, we did.
ASRSN:2279453.s: The pilot reported that wind gusts caused a ground loop on landing, exiting the runway and knocking over a light. After confirming no damage, the crew manually pulled the aircraft to the taxiway and taxied back to the hangar.

ASRSN:2279465.n: I completed a power off 180 that was high and landed long. After landing, I began to slow to taxi off the runway, but I was given instruction for a touch and go. I set up for the touch and go, but as I picked up speed I was unable to rotate the aircraft in time. As we approached the end of the runway, I decided to abort the takeoff. The aircraft came to a stop in the field past the runway. I believe I should have trusted my initial decision to taxi off, then taxi back to the runway instead of initiating the touch and go. Moving forward I intend to be more assertive towards my own judgement and limits, make confident decisions, and be more situationally aware. In this case, the terrain surrounding the airport, runway length, atmospheric conditions, and decreased aircraft performance were the main factors I should have considered and continued taxiing off the runway. This was a commercial progress check as part of the syllabus for the Flight Academy at ZZZ1 Airport. The flight was in a Cessna 172P. We took off from ZZZ1 and flew to the East Practice Area. We flew various maneuvers that the progress check required. Afterwards, the plan was to fly to ZZZ2 for various VFR traffic patterns. The syllabus has Diversion has a graded item, so I had the student divert to ZZZ. ZZZ was only 6 miles away within the boundaries of East Practice Area. This would save some time. The student flew over the airport to enter the traffic pattern and I briefed her about being cautious of the short and narrow runway (XX00' long and 60' wide). There is no broadcast weather information for ZZZ. The wind sock indicated about 10 knots from the north. On the first touch and go, I admonished her about delaying the power up for take off because of the short runway. On the second touch and go, she landed long (1400' from threshold). Ounce again, I told her to power up immediately, and she did at my command. At 60 KIAS, she rotated the airplane, but unexpectedly pulled the power to idle and started braking. I took the controls and used maximum braking, but departed the end of runway XX into the grass. We were unhurt, but broke off one end of runway light. With assistance from the airport staff, we turned the airplane around and taxied back on the pavement. The left tire blew out on the pavement, so we were unable to move the plane any further. Eventually, the left wheel was lifted and placed on a dolly and moved to the parking area. Damage to the airplane was minimal. The left tire and transponder antenna needed replacement.
ASRSN:2279465.s: During a commercial progress check in a Cessna 172P at ZZZ Airport, a student pilot aborted a touch-and-go after landing long, resulting in an overrun into the grass. The incident caused minimal aircraft damage, including a blown tire and broken runway light, attributed to delayed rotation and poor decision-making regarding the short runway.

ASRSN:2279466.n: A drone flew over the left wing of our Diamond DV20 after completing steep turns. The drone was at an altitude of 3000 ft MSL. There was no position lighting or warning from ADS-B or TCAS. The drone was a 4 propeller drone and was directly over the end of the left wing. It was not seen again after flying in a 360. The position and altitude were reported to ZZZ Approach. The student in the left seat was able to identify the drone as something that appeared to a DJI Phantom drone.
ASRSN:2279466.s: A drone flew over the left wing of a Diamond DV20 at 3000 ft MSL during steep turns, with no ADS-B or TCAS warning. The student pilot identified it as a DJI Phantom, and the incident was reported to ZZZ Approach.

ASRSN:2279485.n: While creating a video of a group of people who were posing for the video, I transitioned the drone over 3 or 4 members of the group. This was done to create a pull-back reveal shot, starting from an open space encircled by the people and transitioning to a location outside the group.My understanding that sustained flight over people is not allowed but transitioning over is allowed. After a couple days I began questioning my understanding of 'transitioning'. After re-reading the relevant part 107 operations, I have some uncertainty over whether my actions may have constituted a deviation from the rules of part 107.
ASRSN:2279485.s: A Part 107 remote pilot flew a drone over three to four people to create a video pull-back shot, believing transitioning was permitted. The pilot later questioned if this action constituted a deviation from Part 107 rules regarding sustained flight over people.

ASRSN:2279513.n: I was the pilot flying and my captain was the pilot monitoring.We descended from 34000 to 26000 for smoother rides towards ZZZ1 as per ATC .Once we got there in about 10 min or so just short of ZZZ we heard a loud bang and multiple less louder bangs after. At this point we knew we would possibly have an engine 2 compressor stall.We initially got the ECAM (Electronic Centralized Aircraft Monitor), and the captain split the duties. I was PF already so he told me to fly and tell ATC what's going on and our plans.As the captain started the ECAM, one of the first steps were verify engine 2 idle and as soon as he did that the ECAM went away. He contacted the dispatcher, maintenance, kept the FA informed [with a] brief, and the passengers.After that I requested priority handling and we ran the rest of our checklist, briefed up and the captain decided to land the plane.Once we landed safely, we were met by firetrucks and then we safely taxied to the gate.
ASRSN:2279513.s: The pilot flying and captain experienced a loud bang and suspected engine 2 compressor stall while descending to 26,000 feet near ZZZ1. After the ECAM warning cleared upon verifying idle thrust, the crew requested priority handling, landed safely, and taxied to the gate with fire trucks present.

ASRSN:2279560.n: Assigned Gate XX. On Airport Moving Map (AMM) and 10-9 charts, location of [Gate] XX incorrect. Newly completed Gate XX location needs to be updated. Gate XX in Albany is not depicted correctly on the Jepp chart or Airport Moving Map (AMM). It is located on the west side of Concourse, A, not the east side.
ASRSN:2279560.s: A pilot reported that Gate XX at Albany is incorrectly depicted on the Airport Moving Map and Jepp charts as being on the east side of Concourse A. The gate is actually located on the west side, requiring an update to the charts and moving map.

ASRSN:2279600.n: On a visual approach to Runway XXL, we intercepted final above the GS and were correcting. We were instructed to maintain 170KTS until a 5 mile final. While descending in landing configuration, I noticed that I had not set target AS inside of the 5 miles. I set target and was slowing when we went slightly below the GS and got a low altitude alert from ATC. We were already correcting back to the GS and were stable on speed at 1300'MSL. Normal landing in the touchdown zone.
ASRSN:2279600.s: The flight crew on a visual approach to Runway XXL descended below the glide slope while slowing from 170 knots, triggering a low altitude alert from ATC. They corrected back to the glide slope, stabilized at 1300 feet MSL, and completed a normal landing in the touchdown zone.

ASRSN:2279641.n: During landing, in the rollout phase, after applying the brakes, they remained locked, causing the tires to burst. The aircraft came to a stop on the runway without further consequences. The passengers were disembarked and taken to the terminal. After Maintenance replaced the tires and brakes, I was able to taxi the aircraft to the standBrakes locked. I was the pilot flying the during the flight from ZZZ1 to ZZZ. We were conducting a visual approach to XXL and asked to maintain best forward speed as long as we could to provide the needed separation from the aircraft behind us. So, I was conducting a standard high speed approach coming into ZZZ. The winds were about 90 degrees from the landing runway with perhaps a minimal tailwind component. We were asked to LAHSO Runway XYL for crossing traffic which we accepted, knowing the any tailwind was negligible, we had acceptable weather conditions, etc. I crossed the threshold at about 100 kts. I touched down at the first set of 500' markers beyond the aiming points and began the rollout using aerodynamic and traditional breaking. At this point, the brakes seemed to be functioning normally. The Captain asked for and we exchanged control of the aircraft. He began braking and asked me to not apply brake pressure. I responded that I wasn't on the brakes, and in fact had my feet flat on the floor. The Captain brought the plane to a stop on the runway. When we attempted to exit the runway the plane would not move under its own power. Both the Captain and I didn't have any travel in our brakes, and they felt locked. We were later informed that both tires were flat. When the aircraft was jacked, neither tire would spin freely. Cause: Post-landing inspection revealed that neither main gear wheel would freely rotate. This lack of rotation likely caused accelerated, excessive wear on the main tires which caused both to become flat. Excessive friction and the ensuant elevated temperature during breaking may have caused the brake pads to bind to the wheel rotors. Although I do not believe excess brake pressure was applied, it does seem that the brakes locked right around or before the time of the change of flight controls.
ASRSN:2279641.s: The pilot flying reported that during the rollout after a high-speed landing, the brakes locked and both main tires burst. Post-landing inspection indicated excessive friction likely caused the brake pads to bind to the rotors, preventing wheel rotation and resulting in flat tires.

ASRSN:2279644.n: Crew arrived at the aircraft 1 hour prior to departure. Due to Maintenance actions, flight blocked out almost 3 hours after scheduled departure time of XA:00. Upon logbook review and Maintenance briefing it was noted on the previous 2 flights there was the same discrepancy of HYD OVHT SYS 4. Maintenance advised crew that the discrepancy had been taken care of along with other deferrals and the aircraft was signed off airworthy.During climb out from ZZZ crew received EICAS message DOOR ELEC MAIN. PM referenced the QRH as the other 2 pilots observed and the onboard mechanic was also advised. Checklist was completed and pressurization was normal and flight continued toward destination. Reaching cruise altitude the Observer seat pilot left the cockpit to start his rest. Approximately 1 hour into the flight at cruise altitude FL330 an EICAS message of HYD OVHT SYS 4 was received. QRH was accomplished and per the checklist Engine driven and Demand pumps 4 were turned off. It was noted that the SYS 4 temperature began to come down but was still high forcing the system 4 to remain depressurized. Captain gave flight controls to FO and initiated a SATCOM call with Dispatch and Maintenance Control. Maintenance Control requested the aircraft be brought back to ZZZ and Dispatcher and Captain agreed as this was the safest course of action due to loss of many systems and abnormal configurations and with the most resources to address the problem instead of continuing to original scheduled departure station of ZZZZ. The relief pilot on rest was called back to the flight deck and assisted with checklists.A reanalysis by Dispatched was received and new routing coordinated with ATC back to ZZZ. Maintenance requested fuel dumping and this was accomplished bringing the landing weight under MGLW. ATC was also advised due the maintenance status of the aircraft. The aircraft was configured early and landed on Runway XXR in ZZZ. Aircraft taxied to parking and did receive a BRAKE TEMP EICAS message. A post-flight inspection was completed finding no damage and appropriate logbook discrepancies were annotated.Cause: Unsure of cause of HYD OVHT SYS 4 EICAS message but this was the 3rd flight in a row with the same discrepancy.
ASRSN:2279644.s: The crew experienced a recurring HYD OVHT SYS 4 EICAS message at FL330, prompting a return to ZZZ after maintenance advised it was the safest option. The aircraft dumped fuel, landed safely, and post-flight inspection found no damage, though the cause of the third consecutive hydraulic overheat remains unknown.

ASRSN:2279650.n: Aircraft X was parked at [Gate] XX. The aircraft pushed back and was cleared to taxi. Shortly after contacting ground we were cleared to turn left on Alpha taxiway then Alpha 13, Victor, Victor 6, November for runway 22L. I looked left and said clear left and the FO looked right and said clear right. After adding power and moving a few feet onto the taxiway the FO directed me to stop because of Aircraft Y on Alpha taxiway taxiing at a high rate of speed. ATC did not instruct us to wait for that aircraft or inform us it was coming. I applied brakes to stop the aircraft to ensure we would not contact that aircraft, which was a sudden stop. As soon as I stopped and we were clear of the aircraft I called back to the flight attendants to check on them and see if they were up. I was informed the number X flight attendant fell down and possibly hurt her foot. I asked if she needed or wanted to go back to the gate. Another flight attendant also said that we have reserves and not to worry if she had to get off the flight. I said again it wasn't a big deal and we can go back. She said it wasn't that bad. I was informed everyone else was okay. I checked on them again after climbing thru 18,000' the number X said it was a little sore, but that's it. After landing, I talked to the number 3 and she said she iced it a little and that it was a little sore. All flight attendants continued on their scheduled flight back to Chicago with two different pilots as originally scheduled.Cause: ATC ground control could have either informed us of that aircraft taking on Alpha or told us to follow them. After contacting ground control for our initial taxi clearance from the ramp area in ORD, I cleared the area to the right of the aircraft and the CA advanced power to start the initial roll out of the ramp area. I again looked to the right of the aircraft to ensure we were still clear and saw Aircraft Y taxiing at a high rate of speed around the curve of taxiway A. ATC had made no mention of this aircraft in our initial taxi instructions. I told the Captain to stop and he looked to the right in my direction and immediately spotted the high speed taxiing aircraft. He quickly applied the brakes to stop our slow movement and the aircraft came to a surprisingly quick stop. After the crossing traffic passed us the CA immediately called the flight attendants to ensure everyone was ok because of our quick stop. The number 3 FA informed him that she had fallen and possibly hurt her foot during the stop but felt ok continuing the flight and would monitor her foot for worsening symptoms. We continued our taxi and the flight completed without further incident as the CA called a few times during the flight to check on the FA's wellbeing. The CA and I left the FA crew in ZZZ for our overnight and they continued back to ORD with another crew. Cause: ATC failed to mention or missed Aircraft Y's high rate of taxi speed.
ASRSN:2279650.s: During taxi at ORD, the crew of Aircraft X stopped suddenly to avoid a high-speed Aircraft Y on Taxiway Alpha, which ATC failed to mention in clearance. The abrupt stop caused a flight attendant to fall and injure her foot, though she continued the flight without further incident.

ASRSN:2279711.n: We reported on time for ZZZ-ZZZZ, the inbound aircraft arrived late. Upon arrival at the gate, we conferred with the deplaning Captain regarding the active MEL XX-XX-XXX (Right HP Shutoff Valve - Closed), which had been applied on the previous leg in ZZZZ1.My FO (First Officer) and I thoroughly reviewed and complied with the MEL, including all O and M procedures.Departure and initial climb were uneventful. While climbing through approximately FL200, we received a R BLEED OVHT caution. I was Pilot Flying (PF), my FO was Pilot Monitoring (PM) and initiated the ECL (Electronic Checklist). The ECL directs selecting R BLEED OFF, which was already selected off due to the MEL. No further ECL actions were applicable.Although compliant with MEL procedures, we were concerned about the overheat indication on a system that should have been isolated per MEL. With no effective guidance in the ECL and an active caution, I directed the FO to contact Maintenance Control via SAT phone while I continued flying and handled VHF comms.Maintenance Control advised manually closing the crossbleed valve to isolate the bleed system further. After closing the crossbleed, the OVHT indication persisted. This also disabled anti-ice protection on the right wing, a concern due to enroute weather and potential icing conditions ahead over Location A.While evaluating options with Maintenance and Dispatch, we received a R PACK FAIL caution, several minutes after closing the crossbleed valve. Despite the pack lacking a bleed air source, we ran the ECL to verify no relevant procedural guidance was missed. • With the R PACK selected OFF, duct pressure remained normal. • With the R PACK selected AUTO, duct pressure dropped (~9 PSI), and the PACK symbol remained amber. The caution returned. • This raised concern over a potential leaking valve.Shortly after, while level at FL300, we began experiencing strong, abnormal trim air surges into the cockpit, with duct temps reaching 194°F. These surges were more intense and erratic than typical when operating with MEL'd PRV (pressure relief valves). With cockpit temperatures rising rapidly and no guidance in the ECL, we became increasingly concerned about the escalating behavior in the single-bleed, single-pack configuration and potential further system degradation.My FO suggested turning Trim Air OFF, which I agreed to. This action immediately stopped the abnormal temperature surges and stabilized the cabin environment.Given the cumulative concerns -- persistent R BLEED OVHT, R PACK FAIL, abnormal trim air behavior, and no guidance available -- we decided along with Maintenance/Dispatch concurrence to return to ZZZ. We requested priority handling due to the current system anomalies and anticipated overweight landing. We requested and were cleared to descend to 10,000 ft as a precaution in case of further pressurization loss.At approximately 10,000 ft, the R BLEED OVHT caution cleared.We coordinated with ATC for a return to ZZZ, selecting Runway XXR due to its length and favorable wind alignment (winds 140 degrees). We completed the Overweight Landing ECL and briefed the Inflight crew and customers.I conducted an ILS XXR approach in visual conditions. The aircraft landed Flaps 5 with LO autobrakes, transitioning to light manual braking and maximum reverse. Touchdown was smooth (~150 FPM), well within the TDZ. Aircraft weight was ~141,000 lbs (VREF: 137 + 5). Brake temps were normal, highest at 05. Emergency equipment was staged as a precaution.We taxied to the gate uneventfully. CFR (Crash Fire Rescue) met us at the gate and confirmed no abnormal indications remained. No further assistance was needed.Logbook entries were made for the aircraft indications and overweight landing.
ASRSN:2279711.s: The flight crew experienced a right bleed overheat and pack failure while climbing through FL200 on a ZZZ-ZZZZ flight, likely caused by a leaking valve despite MEL compliance. They returned to ZZZ for an overweight landing after turning trim air off to stop abnormal cockpit temperature surges.

ASRSN:2279721.n: During this flight, me and an instructor were taking off XXL, and experienced a brief ECU B failure, which lasted about 3 seconds before clearing. We took note of this, and continued to ZZZ, our first airport on our route. We landed without incident.After our first takeoff at ZZZ, we noticed that we had a dual ECU (Engine Control Unit) Failure. I immediately pulled out the QRH and followed said checklist to the line, where after introducing 50% power, the ECU A failure cleared, while ECU B remained latched. I intended to land, and run the checklist on the ground, to see if it would clear. The instructor pilot said we should continue with a few touch and go's before making our final decision. After our final approach to landing with the ECU B failure annunciation still latched, I advised we should land and take said checklist action. The instructor pilot said that is not be necessary and we should just take it back to ZZZ1, with ECU B fail annunciation still latched. We flew back to ZZZ1 after a touch and go at ZZZ2 without incident.
ASRSN:2279721.s: A student pilot and instructor experienced a dual ECU failure during training at ZZZ, where ECU B remained latched despite QRH actions. The instructor overruled the student's request to land and instead directed a return to ZZZ1 with the fault still active.

ASRSN:2279740.n: Planned diversion due to loss of oil in the number 1 engine. While conducting post emergency tasks and duties, FO immediately reassigned to continue flight to ZZZ on flight ABC just over 2.5 hrs later. Flight ABC landed in ZZZ over 5 hours past scheduled arrival. Planned diversion due to loss of oil in the number 1 engine. Continuing to deal with post emergency flight duties, the captain was reassigned to continue to operate to ZZZ on flight ABC. From block in to block out was just over 2 1/2 hours. Flight ABC landed in ZZZ just over 5 hours past scheduled arrival.
ASRSN:2279740.s: The crew diverted due to number 1 engine oil loss, then the First Officer and Captain were reassigned to continue flight ABC to ZZZ after a 2.5-hour turnaround. The flight landed over 5 hours late while the crew managed post-emergency duties.

ASRSN:2279744.n: On Day 0 Flight ABC ZZZ to ZZZ1 was operated. During the Captains cockpit preparation flow it was verified that the number one and number two engines had 22 quarts of oil. During the logbook review the Captain and First Officer were aware that the number one engine was being monitored for high oil consumption. During the preflight inspection, the First Officer thoroughly inspected with a flashlight, the interior and exterior of both the number one and number two engines and observed no evidence of oil leaking. The flight taxied out and departed for ZZZ1. Approximately 35 minutes in route the First Officer and Captain recognized the oil quantities were substantially different. The number one engine was indicating 11 1/2 quarts of oil. We begin monitoring the oil quantity level in the number one engine and determined that the engine was losing a half a quart of oil every four minutes. The Captain made a sat phone call to Dispatch and was patched in with Maintenance Control. Both were made aware of the situation and it was determined the flight would not be able to continue to ZZZ1. Dispatch and Maintenance coordinated the decision to go to ZZZ2 as our diversion city. The Captain informed the in-flight crew of the diversion to ZZZ2 and the possibility of shutting down the number one engine. The Captain then made a PA to the customers informing them of our situation and diversion to ZZZ2. There was no code issued at that time. There were no ECAM (Electronic Centralized Aircraft Monitor) messages or abnormal indications, we only had an advisory message when the oil quantity on the number one engine reached 5 quarts. During the descent passing through 22,000 feet the Captain started the APU in preparation for a potential engine shutdown. During the arrival phase into ZZZ2, priority handling was issued by ZZZ Approach on behalf of flight ABC. ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting) equipment was dispatched and awaiting the arrival of flight ABC in ZZZ2. After safely arriving in ZZZ2, the number one engine was indicating one and a half quarts of oil prior to engine shut down at the gate. Once the engine was completely shut down it then indicated 7 quarts. Maintenance met the aircraft at the gate and advised the Captain and First Officer that he observed zero oil in the sight glass.
ASRSN:2279744.s: The flight crew diverted Flight ABC to ZZZ2 due to rapid oil loss in engine one, which dropped from 22 to 1.5 quarts en route. Maintenance confirmed zero oil in the sight glass after shutdown, despite no abnormal ECAM messages during the flight.

ASRSN:2279799.n: The aircraft was on a long maintenance delay due to indicators that came on during the unbound which could have detected the fuel was corrupted and not pure. Not being a maintenance base a non-Company mechanic needed to be called. It took a while for him to arrive, and to run all the diagnostics and clear the aircraft for operation. during the last fifteen minutes of the delay, the gaspers started blowing hot air.We were being cleared by maintenance, and the agents were anxious to board and be relieved of the difficult task of managing the customers. the temps in the back on my unauthorized thermometer was above 91, but the flight deck indicator only registered 72, not constituting a hot plane. The decision was made to board quickly and get the already greatly inconvenienced faster out of there to the hub. Unfortunately, my accurate count was 34+ an infant. Often the gate agents do not have a uniform way of communicating the amount of humans on board when there is a lap child involved. Having had several encounters with this over the summer I verified with the gate agent that the written and circled 35 on the final paperwork was 34+ an infant was correct, there was a little bit of back-and-forth, but I knew the amount of people on the plane so I again asserted that it was 34 seats plus one lap infant equaling 35. The account matched with the flight deck and the door was closed, however, during my announcement prior to the safety demo, the flight deck called and asked me to verify the amount of persons in Section X. Apparently Section X had the correct count, but after the door was closed, and the agent went back up. They added another person to Section X. This became problematic and the door had to be re-opened. The passengers were already extremely hot, but bearing up in order to have an on-time departure and looking forward to cooler air once airborne. But unfortunately, at the door came open, and the heat situation became unbearable as the gate agents called out names and made a roll call. I was during this time that one woman who was a wheelchair passenger and aged 82 was not doing well and had to be brought to the front. A young service man went back and took a seat in her section for those weight and balance purposes. Initially EMTs were on their way, but the woman said she felt much better in the front and did not want to be removed from the plane. The beginning of this flight was miserable, and the people were very angry. By the end of the flight, most of them had calmed down and had a strategy for their connections. However, the plane was unsafely, hot and for an extended amount of time. It was difficult to think. Old planes, a summer filled with horrible heat and horrible delays, and a non-standard way of listing the final count when there is a lap child involved-I have seen several different ways of communicating the final count, and have had to at least clarify. Company issued thermometers for flight attendant to use at out stations, and language in the manuals to allow for accurate readings to be addressed appropriately. No more flying hot planes.
ASRSN:2279799.s: A flight attendant reported that a maintenance delay and subsequent passenger count error caused the aircraft to remain on the ground in extreme heat, leading to an 82-year-old wheelchair passenger becoming ill. The incident highlighted issues with non-standard passenger counting for lap infants and a lack of accurate cabin temperature monitoring equipment.
